newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative Redwood rejects right-wing tag.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative Redwood rejects right-wing tag.

text.p: John Redwood sought on Wednesday to boost his Conservative leadership chances by insisting that he was running a mainstream campaign that would restore the main opposition party's traditional values.

Speaking at a news conference at which he set out his environmental policies, the former Welsh secretary hotly rejected a suggestion that he and his supporters constituted a narrow right-wing faction.

"Look, I'm fed up with all this Right-Left stuff in the Conservative party. We are Conservatives, we believe in some common-sense principles. It is high time we were proud of those principles and got out and told people why we believe in them...

"We have to put behind us this idea that there's a tussle for the party's soul between Right and Left. It was far worse under Margaret Thatcher when we had wets' and dries' arguing over economic policy. We agree about far more things than we disagree about," he said.

Redwood, who is lagging badly in straw polls for the June 10 election, said he was better placed than his five rivals to revive the party because he was not tainted by the government's record in the final run-up to its rout in the May 1 election.
Redwood quit the cabinet in June 1995 to take up John Major's challenge to his critics to "put up or shut up".
"I don't have to defend all of the past. I can get on with the future and this Conservative party has to look to the future," he said.
Bookmakers Ladbrokes on Wednesday made Redwood 14/1 joint fourth favourite with former home secretary Michael Howard.
Ex-Welsh Secretary William Hague is 4/5 favourite but Ladbrokes reported a flood of bets on former chancellor of the exchequer Kenneth Clarke, narrowing his odds to 6/4 from 5/2.
Because of the anti-European bent of many of the 164 Conservative members of parliament who will elect the leader, Clarke's pro-European views made him a rank outsider at 7/1 only a few weeks ago.
"No one wanted to know Kenneth Clarke fourteen days ago, but everyone who is betting on the contest now is betting on Clarke," Ladbrokes spokesman Ed Nicholson said.
Former social security secretary Peter Lilley is third favourite at 5/1. Ex-health secretary Stephen Dorrell makes up the field at 25/1.

In remarks prepared for delivery to Conservative activists in Bristol later on Wednesday, Dorrell said the party had lost contact with its own supporters and had to use its time in opposition to renew its organisation and ideas.

"Party reform is urgent. Membership must be expanded. Central office must be strengthened. Discipline in the party must be tightened, and the membership of the party must be given a proper say in the key decisions facing the party, including future leadership elections," Dorrell said.
